mcqs.question: Why do GPT-style LLMs use a causal (masked) self-attention pattern instead of letting every token attend to every other token?
options: It matches generation, where only past tokens exist — training must mirror that constraint
It makes the attention computation cheaper than bidirectional attention
It prevents the model from learning long-range dependencies, which improves stability
It is required so the tokenizer can process text left to right
mcqs.explanation: The causal mask exists so training matches inference: at generation time a model only ever has the tokens produced so far, never future ones. Option A is false (masking doesn't reduce the underlying quadratic cost). Option C is backwards — long-range dependency modeling is exactly what attention is for. Option D confuses tokenization with attention.

mcqs.question: What problem does byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenization solve that a fixed whole-word vocabulary does not?
options: It guarantees every generated sentence is grammatically correct
It handles rare or unseen words by breaking them into known subword pieces instead of an unknown-word token
It removes the need for the model to use attention
It compresses the model's parameter count directly
mcqs.explanation: BPE builds a vocabulary of frequent subword chunks, so any input — including words never seen during vocabulary construction — can be represented as a sequence of known pieces rather than falling back to an out-of-vocabulary token. It has nothing to do with grammar correctness, attention, or parameter count.

mcqs.question: A team has a fixed compute budget and must choose between training a larger model on fewer tokens or a smaller model on more tokens. What do scaling-law results (Chinchilla-style) suggest?
options: Always maximize parameter count; data quantity barely matters once the model is large enough
Scaling laws only apply below 1 billion parameters and stop predicting anything past that
There's a compute-optimal balance between parameters and training tokens, and many earlier large models were under-trained relative to their size
Training tokens should always be capped at the size of the parameter count to avoid overfitting
mcqs.explanation: Chinchilla-style scaling results showed that, for a fixed compute budget, there's an optimal parameter-to-token ratio, and several earlier large models were oversized relative to the data they were trained on — a smaller, more fully-trained model can beat them. Option A ignores the data side entirely; C and D misstate the actual findings.

mcqs.question: What does KV caching avoid during autoregressive generation?
options: Running the causal mask on the first token of a sequence
Recomputing the token embeddings for the current input prompt only
Loading the model weights from disk between requests
Recomputing the key and value vectors for every previous token at each new generation step
mcqs.explanation: Without caching, generating each new token would require redoing the key/value computation for every prior token, since attention needs them all. KV caching stores those vectors once and reuses them, so each step only computes the new token's own key/value. It doesn't touch weight loading or embeddings of the current prompt.

mcqs.question: A team defaults to the largest available frontier model for a narrow, well-defined classification task inside a latency-sensitive product. What's the most likely mistake?
options: They're overpaying in latency and cost for generality the narrow task doesn't need, when a smaller tuned or prompted model would clear the same quality bar
Frontier models cannot perform simple classification tasks at all
Larger models always produce less accurate results on narrow tasks
Frontier models cannot be used at all for latency-sensitive products
mcqs.explanation: Scale buys general capability, not a free win on every task — a smaller, well-prompted or fine-tuned model can often match a frontier model on a narrow job at a fraction of the cost and latency. Options A, C, and D overstate the case; frontier models usually still work, they're just an inefficient choice here.

mcqs.question: Why does RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) make it easier to extend a model's context window after pretraining, compared to adding a fixed absolute position vector?
options: RoPE encodes relative position through rotation, so query/key dot products naturally reflect distance between tokens, and the rotation frequencies can be rescaled for longer sequences without retraining from scratch
RoPE removes the need for positional information entirely, so context length becomes irrelevant
RoPE only works up to a fixed, hard-coded context length that can never be changed
RoPE replaces self-attention with a cheaper convolution operation
mcqs.explanation: RoPE rotates query and key vectors by an angle tied to position, so the resulting dot product encodes relative distance rather than an absolute lookup — this relative structure is what lets the rotation frequencies be rescaled to stretch context length after the fact. It doesn't eliminate the need for position information, isn't hard-capped, and has nothing to do with convolutions.
